title: Podcasting
summary: Plan, record and grow a podcast: show concepts and formats, equipment and recording space, hosting and interviewing, editing, loudness and file sizes, publishing, promotion and analytics, and sponsorship, ethics and sustainability. Calculations were checked in code.
audience: Aspiring podcasters, journalists, educators, churches, NGOs and businesses

body.p: A podcast is a series of audio (or video) episodes that people can stream or download and listen to on demand. Podcasts work well for interviews, storytelling, education, news analysis, faith, business and comedy, and listening is growing across Africa as data costs fall and phones improve.

list: Topic and angle: what is your show about, and what makes it different?
Audience: who is it for, and when and where will they listen (commuting, at work, at home)?
Format: solo, co-hosted, interview, panel, narrative storytelling or a mix.
Length and frequency: for example 30 minutes every week. Consistency matters more than length.
Language: English, French, Swahili, Yoruba, Zulu or a mix; podcasts in local languages often find loyal audiences with little competition.

body.p: Plan at least six to ten episode ideas before launching. If you cannot think of ten, the concept may be too narrow.

body.tip: Name your show so listeners can guess the topic from the title; clever names that need explaining are hard to find in search.

list: Microphone: a dynamic USB microphone is affordable and rejects room noise, ideal for home recording. Even a phone with a lapel microphone can sound good.
Headphones: closed-back headphones let you monitor sound without the microphone picking it up.
Recording software: free tools such as Audacity or GarageBand, or a phone recording app; online platforms record remote guests on separate tracks.
Optional: an audio interface and XLR microphones, a portable recorder for interviews outside.

body.h: Your room matters more than gear

body.p: Hard, empty rooms create echo. Record in a small room with soft furnishings, such as curtains, a bed, a sofa or clothes in a wardrobe. Switch off fans, fridges and air conditioners if possible, silence phones and choose quiet times of day.
Speak about a fist's width from the microphone, slightly off-axis to reduce popping sounds, and keep the same distance throughout. Record a short test and listen back before every session.

body.tip: Always record a backup: a second phone recording can save an episode if the main recording fails.

list: Speak as if talking to one listener, not a crowd.
Prepare an outline with key points, not a full script, unless the format needs one; reading word for word often sounds flat.
Most people speak about 150 words a minute, so a 30-minute episode is about 4500 words of conversation.
Vary pace and tone, smile while you talk, and pause instead of saying "um".

steps: Research your guest and their work.
Send the topic and format in advance, and agree on recording logistics.
Prepare open questions that start with how, why or tell me about, and follow-ups.
Listen actively and follow interesting answers instead of rushing to the next question.
Ask for stories and specific examples.
Thank the guest and tell them when the episode will be published.

body.tip: Get each guest's written consent to record and publish, especially for sensitive topics.

steps: Remove long pauses, false starts and off-topic sections, while keeping a natural conversational feel.
Balance volume so all voices are at similar levels.
Apply gentle noise reduction, EQ and compression to make voices clear and even.
Add intro and outro music and any segments, using music you have rights to.
Normalise loudness: many platforms recommend around -16 LUFS for stereo podcasts.

body.p: File size depends on bitrate. At 128 kbps, a 30-minute (1800 s) episode is 128 x 1800 / 8 = 28 800 kilobytes, about 28.8 MB. A 64 kbps mono file is about 14.4 MB, cheaper to download for listeners on limited data, and fine for speech.

body.tip: Create a template project with your music, levels and effects so each new episode is quicker to edit.

body.p: Podcasts are distributed through a hosting service that creates an RSS feed. You submit the feed once to directories such as Spotify, Apple Podcasts, YouTube and others, and new episodes then appear automatically.

list: Artwork: a clear, square image that reads well when small.
Titles and descriptions: say what each episode is about, using words people search for; include guest names and timestamps.
Launch with three episodes so new listeners can binge.
Promote clips: share short audiogram or video clips on social media and WhatsApp.
Ask guests to share their episodes, and appear as a guest on other podcasts.

body.p: Hosting services show downloads, where listeners are and which apps they use. If an episode gets 2000 downloads and 300 come from a guest's social post, that guest drove 15% of listening, a sign to strengthen partnerships.

body.tip: Publish on the same day and time each week so listeners build a habit.

list: Sponsorships and host-read adverts, priced by audience size and loyalty.
Listener support: memberships, donations and premium episodes.
Selling your own services, courses or products to your audience.
Grants and partnerships with NGOs, media houses or organisations for educational or public-interest podcasts.
Live events and paid workshops.

body.p: Check facts, correct mistakes openly, and clearly separate opinion from fact. Avoid defamation: false statements that damage a person's reputation can lead to lawsuits. Disclose sponsorships. Respect privacy, especially when discussing children, health and victims of crime.
A year of weekly episodes is about 48 to 52 episodes. Plan breaks between seasons, for example four seasons of 12 episodes, so you do not burn out.

body.tip: Treat your podcast as a project with a plan, budget and schedule; it makes consistency much easier.
